newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to launch anti-graft campaign.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to launch anti-graft campaign.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin will call for a tough anti-graft campaign in his annual state of the nation address on Thursday, reviving a theme which once helped him on his way to the Kremlin.

"We have declared war on the economic crime and corruption but have not started it for real," he says in the text, obtained by Reuters on Wednesday. It will be presented to parliament on Thursday, when Yeltsin will make a speech based on the document.

Yeltsin, 66, who campaigned fiercely in the late 1980s against the corrupt and ineffective communist system, has now been forced to admit that in the five years of market reforms he has failed to stamp out organised corruption in Russia's economy.

"In 1992, Russia had only one way to save its economy from collapse -- to put its faith in the power of economic liberty," he said in the address. "(But) market relations have established themselves in sectors where they should be a taboo."

"When free buying and selling extends to the passing of laws, to the work of civil servants and to court decisions, it is not just immoral but a mortal danger to society and the state," said Yeltsin, who was himself a top communist official.

The president, who had heart bypass surgery last November and went down with pneumonia in January, is expected to use his first major public appearance since his re-election last July to reassert his authority over his subordinates.
"Power which is not limited by law is dangerous, while law which is not backed by power is impotent," he said. "Our choice is order based on law."
Yeltsin said the flourishing of mafia-style crime gangs and official corruption had become a major threat to the state.

"The problem of economic crime and corruption have grown from what was clearly a police matter into a political issue," he said. "The criminal world in fact has openly challenged the state and launched into an open competition with it."
Criminal experts say up to 40 percent of Russian businesses are linked to the criminal world or pay protection.
Underworld threats have scared off potential investors, both domestic and foreign, and the flourishing of crime has made millions of Russians feel defenceless and angry.
A string of still unsolved murders of prominent journalists, bankers and politicians has cast doubts about the ability of authotities to control the crime situation.
On Tuesday, Yeltsin gave Chief Prosecutor Yuri Skuratov a public dressing down on television for his failures.
Last month he ordered Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov to coordinate the fight against economic crime and gave him broad powers. But Kulikov has not made public his plans.
Yeltsin said in his address that rooting out economic crime should start with changing conditions which nourish corruption.
He called for changes in the tax system, government structures and business management in a bid to remove incentives for bribery, long the curse of Russian bureaucracy.
Among other things he proposed pay rises for officials to help them resist temptation and recommended setting a proper legal framework for parliamentary lobbyists.

He also demanded harsh punishments. "To fight economic crime and corruption effectively we need to expose those who initiate and organise crimes, the so-called godfathers, rather than just those who merely carry them out," he said.
